https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A slide-deck presentation delivered to the Troy Board of Education at the special meeting held August 12, 2020 (4:00 PM), setting out the Troy School District's recommendation to begin the 2020-21 school year under a fully virtual instructional model in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Return to Learn goals stated at the outset: students return to face-to-face instruction as soon as possible; safety and sustainability; and consistent programming. The district's Return to Learn process is anchored in the MI Return to School Roadmap, guidance from public health experts, and a commitment to remain flexible to changing conditions.

The TSD COVID Preparedness and Response Plan is described as resting on four key elements: County Health Department guidance (Oakland County, regional, and Michigan levels), Safety Protocols, Budget, and Health Data.

The virtual model is branded "ONETroy Virtual Learning" and organized around five key ideas: (1) ONETroy Community at the Center, a caring environment promoting the social and emotional well-being of all students and families; (2) Troy School District Curriculum, described as a world-class curriculum with a common pacing guide, improved instructional tools, and supports for families; (3) Live Daily Instruction, with teachers providing live daily lessons that are also recorded for flexibility on consistent schedules; (4) Meaningful Interactions with Teachers and Classmates, featuring ongoing teacher-to-student feedback, academic grades, student-to-student interaction, and a daily attendance expectation; and (5) Streamlined Technology and Support, using the Schoology learning management system K-12 with a streamlined interface for family support, Zoom as the common platform for live lessons, technology tools available for all TSD students K-12, and parent learning sessions for tech tips. The presentation restates that the district's mission is to ensure learning for ALL students and notes teams are discussing ways to bring the most vulnerable students in at the right time, with the model designed to be adaptive across virtual, transition, or face-to-face settings.

Scheduling details: Elementary schedules feature a common start time for all 12 schools, live (also recorded) lessons, and built-in student supports. Secondary schedules feature a common start time for middle and high schools, live lessons, 90-minute blocks, and an A/B daily schedule with built-in supports. A draft secondary virtual schedule shows an 8:00-9:30 first block, breaks of 15 minutes, a 9:45-11:15 block, a 30-minute break/lunch, and an 11:45-1:15 block, followed by student support and teacher team collaboration/professional learning. The block schedule rotation has classes meeting five times over a two-week rotation, alternating A Day (hours 1-3) and B Day (hours 4-6) across Monday through Friday.

The "Welcome Week" beginning August 24 will include student class assignments, finalized schedules, information on material pick-up, information for welcoming students at sixth and ninth grades, and a special welcome for OneTroy Kindergarten families. Next steps identified include addressing challenges faced by students receiving special education services, exploring solutions for students who need care, building-level communication, and convening task force teams to monitor and plan for transition. The Survey, Evaluate & Transition phase calls for continually watching key metrics (positivity rate, 7-day case average, trend lines, hospitalizations and deaths), surveying parents, evaluating at five weeks, continuing mitigation measures, and transitioning/turning the dial as appropriate.

The plan identifies the district (4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098; District Code 63150; ISD Oakland Schools; authorizing body the Troy Board of Education) and sets out a series of legally required assurances, including equal in-person and remote access for students with disabilities under their IEPs, continued employee pay, continued food distribution, and cooperation with the local health department on contact tracing.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Troy School District's official COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan for 2020-21, dated August 12, 2020, adopted under Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142.

District identifiers
- Name: Troy School District
- Address: 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098
- District Code Number: 63150
- Web: www.troy.k12.mi.us
- Intermediate School District: Oakland Schools
- Authorizing body: Troy Board of Education

Regulatory framework
- EO 2020-142 requires each district to adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan across phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan, guided by the Michigan Return to School Roadmap
- Districts retain flexibility to tailor instruction to regional disease conditions
- No in-person instruction permitted in Phases 1-3; in-person resumes in Phase 4

Key assurances the district agrees to
- Provide in-person instruction to students with disabilities (per IEPs) whenever offering it to students without disabilities
- Strive in good faith to give equal access to alternative instruction for students with disabilities birth-age 26, including auxiliary services under MCL 380.1296
- Comply with US Dept. of Education (OCR, OSERS) and Michigan Dept. of Education guidance
- Make individualized determinations on compensatory services for 2019-20 closures
- During Phases 1-3, close buildings except for essential staff/contractors, food-service workers, and licensed child-care providers; suspend athletics, activities, and busing; continue employee pay and food distribution
- During Phase 4, prohibit indoor assemblies mixing students from more than one classroom
- Cooperate with the local health department and collect close-contact information for confirmed cases
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District's official COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan for the 2020-2021 school year, dated August 12, 2020, and presented to the Board at the August 12 special meeting. The plan was adopted to comply with Governor Gretchen Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142.

District identifying information: Name of District, Troy School District; Address, 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098; District Code Number, 63150; Web Address, www.troy.k12.mi.us; Name of Intermediate School District, Oakland Schools; Name of Authorizing Body, Troy Board of Education.

Preparedness Plan Introduction: The plan quotes Executive Order 2020-142, which provides a structure to support all Michigan schools as they plan for a return of pre-K-12 education in the fall. Under the order, districts must adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan laying out how they will cope with the disease across the phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan, with the accompanying Michigan Return to School Roadmap offering a guide to appropriate safety protocols during each phase. The order emphasizes there is no one-size-fits-all solution and that districts retain flexibility to tailor instruction to their particular needs and regional disease conditions.

Preparedness Plan Assurances: The Troy School District agrees to meet all requirements of EO 2020-142, including: (1) when providing in-person instruction to students without disabilities, it must also provide in-person instruction to students with disabilities consistent with their individualized education programs (IEPs); (2) when schools are closed to in-person instruction, it will strive in good faith and to the extent practicable, based on available resources, technology, training, and curriculum, to provide equal access to alternative modes of instruction to students with disabilities from birth through age 26, including auxiliary services under section 1296 of the Revised School Code, MCL 380.1296; (3) it will comply with guidance from the U.S. Department of Education (including its Office of Civil Rights and Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services) and the Michigan Department of Education regarding alternative instruction for students with disabilities; (4) it will make individualized determinations, to the extent practicable and necessary, whether and to what extent compensatory services may be needed for students with disabilities in light of the 2019-2020 school closures; (5) during Phases 1, 2, or 3 of the Michigan Safe Start Plan it will close buildings to anyone except district employees or contractors necessary for minimum basic school operations (including those facilitating alternative modes of instruction such as distributing materials and equipment), food-service workers preparing food for distribution to students or families, and licensed child-care providers and the families they serve following state emergency protocols; (6) during Phases 1-3 it will suspend athletics, after-school activities, inter-school activities, and busing; (7) during Phases 1-3 it will provide for continued pay of school employees while redeploying staff to meaningful work, subject to any applicable collective bargaining agreement; (8) during Phases 1-3 it will continue food distribution to eligible students; (9) during Phase 4 it will prohibit indoor assemblies that bring together students from more than one classroom; and (10) it will cooperate with the local public health department if a confirmed case of COVID-19 is identified, collecting contact information for close contacts from two days before symptoms appeared until the individual was last present in school.

Preparedness Plan framework: Governor Whitmer will continue to use the MI Safe Start Plan as the highest-level governing framework for determining if and when it is safe to resume in-person instruction. Schools are not permitted to provide in-person instruction of any kind if their region is within Phases 1-3, and all schools are permitted to resume in-person instruction beginning in Phase 4 of the MI Safe Start Plan.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is a concise board action/policy statement, Item 5.D., titled "Virtual Courses Allowance," presented at the August 18, 2020 Regular Meeting of the Troy Board of Education.

The statement provides that all traditional seated courses are eligible to be delivered as virtual courses, or a combination thereof (i.e., hybrid delivery), for the 2020-2021 school year, following the guidelines provided within the Michigan Department of Education (MDE) Pupil Accounting Manual.

It further directs that district and school administration shall coordinate and monitor the implementation of virtual learning and the adherence to state pupil accounting requirements, including student accessibility to virtual learning, attendance, and participation in lessons and assessments.

The measure is part of the district's COVID-19-era planning for the 2020-2021 school year, ensuring that instruction can be offered virtually or in hybrid form while preserving compliance with the state's pupil accounting rules that govern how student enrollment and attendance are counted for funding purposes. The document is brief and administrative in nature, containing no dollar amounts, named individuals, or recorded vote outcome in the extracted text.

What it is
The proposed amended Bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), dated July 2020, provided to member districts (including Troy) for review with the amendment ballot. Prior adoption dates noted: Board of Directors 11/15/2017; General Membership 01/24/2018 and 10/18/2018.

Key provisions
- Article I (Offices): Principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, Oakland County, Michigan; maintains a registered office and registered agent.
- Article II (Purpose): Advance quality of public education in Oakland County through cooperative efforts of locally-elected boards; promote standards, share information, sponsor meetings in partnership with Oakland Schools, and advocate for legislation supporting public education.
- Article III (Membership): Open to any publicly elected Oakland County school district or Oakland ISD board member who is also a MASB member in good standing; one vote per member on most matters; each Member School District gets one vote on committee-chair selection, resolutions (Article IX), and bylaw amendments (Article XVI); electronic voting limited to the Board of Directors for emergency business.
- Article IV (Dues): Financed by an annual MASB grant to CASBA members, ISD membership dues not exceeding the MASB CASBA grant, and contributions/gifts.
- Article V (Meetings): Annual meeting plus at least three additional regular membership meetings yearly; special meetings on 30 days' notice.

Purpose
Governing document defining OCSBA's structure, membership, and operations.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This document is the proposed (July 2020) amended Bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), circulated to member districts including the Troy Board of Education for review in connection with the August 18, 2020 regular meeting and the accompanying Member District amendment ballot. A header notes prior adoptions: by the Board of Directors on 11/15/2017 and by the General Membership on 01/24/2018 and 10/18/2018.

Article I (Offices): Section 1 places the Association's principal office in Michigan at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland, allowing other offices as the Board of Directors may determine. Section 2 requires the Association to continuously maintain a registered office and a registered agent whose office is identical with the registered office, changeable by the Board of Directors.

Article II (Purpose): Section 1 enumerates the Association's purposes: (a) advance the quality of public education in Oakland County through cooperative efforts of locally-elected boards of education; (b) promote high standards in educational programs and services for all students; (c) make information about educational issues available to school board members; (d) conduct and sponsor meetings and programs in partnership with Oakland Schools; (e) promote public understanding of the role of school boards and the need for citizen involvement; (f) enhance cooperation and communication among Oakland County boards of education; (g) present a strong force representing the views of Oakland County school boards to political representatives; and (h) advocate for county, state, and national legislation and governance supporting public education served by locally elected boards.

Article III (Membership): Section 1 organizes the Association on a membership basis, with eligibility open to any publicly elected Board of Education member of an Oakland County school district or any elected Oakland ISD Board of Education member ("Member School Districts") that is also a member in good standing of the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB). Section 2 (Voting Rights) grants each Member one vote on each matter, with all voting done in person, and specifies that each Member School District has one vote on any proposal to select a committee chair, vote on resolutions (Article IX), or amend the Bylaws (Article XVI); such votes are recorded upon receipt of the completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of the district's Trustees and must be received before the stated deadline, with results provided to all Member Districts no later than the next general membership meeting. Section 3 limits electronic voting to the Board of Directors for emergency business, to be reaffirmed at its next meeting. Section 4 states membership is not transferable or assignable.

Article IV (Dues): The Association is financed by an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, Intermediate School District membership dues not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant, and by contributions and gifts accepted by the Association.

Article V (Meeting of Members): Section 1 requires an annual meeting plus at least three additional regular membership meetings each year to appoint the Board of Directors and transact business, with the annual meeting being the first regular meeting after July 1. Section 2 allows special meetings called by voice or email by the President or by two or more Board members with 30 days' notice. Section 3 lets the Board designate the meeting place; absent designation, meetings occur at the registered office, and a meeting is valid without call or notice if all Members meet and consent. The extracted text is truncated within Article V.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is the "Summary of the Proposed 2020 Bylaws Amendments" for the Oakland County School Board Association (OCSBA), as recommended by its Resolutions and Bylaws Committee and Board of Directors, provided to the Troy Board of Education for the August 18, 2020 regular meeting in connection with the member-district vote (August 1 - September 11, 2020). It is a two-page table organized by Article, Section, Page, Proposed Revision, and Rationale, with the note BOD = Board of Directors.

Proposed amendments include: Article V, Section 2 (page 3) - remove "Board or," since special meetings of the Board are addressed elsewhere (Article VII, Section 3). Article VI, Section 3 (page 4) - four changes: (1) remove all nomination language and rename "nomination" forms to "candidate application" forms, because candidates apply and run rather than being nominated; (2) describe the Election Committee as the three most recently elected BOD members; (3) remove nominations from the floor, giving candidates adequate time to apply and eliminating the need for paper ballots (never used and a concern during the pandemic online election); and (4) add a process to seek candidates and appoint for one year when there are fewer candidates than vacancies. Article VI, Section 4 (page 4) - remove "either" and "or without" so that once elected, a BOD member may only be removed for cause. Article VI, Section 5 (page 5) - change "Nomination" to "Candidate Application" Form for consistency. Article VI, Section 6 (page 5) - add that a Director may request an excused absence in writing to the Board President within thirty (30) days of the missed meeting, defining a previously undefined process. Article VII, Section 6 (page 6) - change "present" to "serving (whether elected or appointed)," so BOD actions require a majority of the whole nine-member BOD (5 of 9), like school boards, rather than a majority of members present.

Additional amendments: Article VIII, Section 2 (page 6) - remove "or without," so officers are removed only for cause. Article VIII, Section 4 (page 7) - remove the last sentence (designating another presiding officer in the President's absence) because it conflicts with Section 5, under which the Vice President assumes the President's duties. Article VIII, Section 5 (page 7) - add a paragraph providing that, in the absence of both the President and Vice President, the Directors present shall designate another presiding officer (a chain of command). Article IX, Section 1 (page 8) - add "and ad hoc" to specifically address ad hoc committees not currently described. Article IX, Section 3 (page 8) - change "twice" to "once" and remove "At least three" and "in June" for least-restrictive language. Article XI, Section 1 (page 10) - add a third signatory: in the event the President and/or Treasurer are absent or disabled, the Vice President may serve as signatory and approve expenditures (added due to COVID-19). Article XI, Sections 3a/3b (page 10) - describe an annual internal financial review using agreed-upon procedures conducted by the Association Vice President, Oakland Schools Controller, and the incoming and outgoing OCSBA Treasurers, with an external audit only if required by law or a third party. Article XVI, Section 2 (page 16) - add "unless a local, state or national emergency has been declared" (COVID-19). Article XVI, Section 3 (page 16) - add a new Section 3, "Rules and Regulations During a Declared Emergency," allowing the Board of Directors to set aside bylaws rules and regulations regarding meetings, elections, and the conduct of Association affairs during a declared emergency (added due to COVID-19, after the Association was required to hold a fourth meeting and a Zoom election in June during the pandemic). The OCR text contains some duplicated/garbled lines but the substance of each amendment is preserved.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This memorandum, on Office of the Superintendent letterhead (4400 Livernois; Ph 248.823.4003; Fax 248.823.4012), is dated September 1, 2020, and is addressed from Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., to the Troy Board of Education, with the subject "Proposed Purchasing Policy."

The memo explains that CARES Act and COVID relief funds had recently been released by the federal government and the State of Michigan. While the district was still awaiting specific direction on spending parameters, it knew for certain that the purchase of PPE would be an allowable expense.

To provide the necessary flexibility as the district prepared its offices and buildings for the return of staff and students, Machesky states it was necessary to ask the board for maximum flexibility regarding purchasing powers around COVID-related expenses.

The memo reports that Rick (Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services) had been in contact with Plante Moran and the district's legal counsel to draft a revision to Policy 5000.03 - Purchasing Policy. The draft policy was provided to the board for review. Machesky indicates that the background of the request and the need for the additional language would be discussed during the Workshop, and that, with board support, the revised policy would be included in the Special Board meeting for a second reading and approval.

The memo closes by inviting board members to contact either Rich (Machesky) or Rick (West) with questions in advance. This policy-revision request is directly tied to the same September 1, 2020 special meeting at which the board considered the $34,270.40 acrylic-shield PPE purchase from IMBranded, reflecting the district's effort to adapt its procurement procedures to the rapid, pandemic-driven spending needs of reopening. The memo does not include the text of the proposed policy language itself or a vote outcome.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A capital projects update presentation titled "Troy School District Capital Projects - Bond, BSSF and TLC Fund - Projects Update September 2020," delivered under agenda item 8.B at the September 15, 2020 Regular Board of Education meeting by Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, and Beth Soggs, Director of Technology.

2020 Bond/BSSF Building Improvement Projects included: Hill and Wattles Elementary Schools mechanical upgrades (boilers, unit ventilators, HVAC units), electrical upgrades (panels and fire alarm systems), and kiln room construction; Athens High School pool upgrades and art room renovation; Costello, Martell and IAE stage renovation (ADA accessible ramp and operable partitions); removal of in-wall cafe tables at Costello, Martell and Wattles; Boulan and Larson window and door replacement; Bemis gym/cafe operable wall replacement; Troy Union ADA lift project in the kindergarten wing; the Niles relocation project; and building renovation of the new TSD Learning Center.

Site Improvement Projects covered IAE parking lot replacement/redesign (removal of tennis courts and new LED lighting), Athens student parking lot replacement/redesign (new dedicated entry and exit), Troy High main entrance parking area improvement, and Hill paved play and sidewalk replacements.

Roof Replacement Projects included Athens (pool and main gym roofs), IAE (academic areas, main office and TCT), and Troy High (academic wings, counseling offices, auditorium seating and lobby areas). Flooring Replacement Projects covered Hill and Wattles (classrooms and gym), IAE (cafeteria and stage), and polished concrete and terrazzo at Athens, Smith, Costello and Martell.

Annual Maintenance Projects included district-wide concrete replacement; asphalt patch, sealcoating and parking lot striping; fencing replacement and improvements; and brick/block repair and tuckpointing.

The deck also presented 2014 Bond progress matrices. The elementary matrix (Barnard, Bemis, Costello, Hamilton, Hill, Leonard, Martell, Morse, Schroeder, Troy Union, Wass, Wattles) tracked items such as secure entry vestibules, secure welcome centers, electronic access systems, walkway replacements, parking lot lighting and additions, roofing, door/window upgrades, exterior lighting, building automation, equipment upgrades, electrical infrastructure, fire alarm, and emergency lighting. The secondary matrix (Baker, Boulan Park, Larson, Smith, Athens, Troy High, I.A. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A presentation titled "Update on Equity & Inclusion work" delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education, dated September 1, 2020 and presented at the September 15, 2020 Regular Board meeting. The presenters are Natalie Haezebrouck, Director of Teaching and Learning; Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary; and Kristine Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary. The deck references an Equity Padlet resource.

The presentation frames what Equity and Inclusion work in Troy means: working to recognize biases before making decisions; understanding that equitable and equal are not the same; identifying and addressing opportunity gaps for students; ensuring a sense of belonging for all members of the "OneTroy" community; and upholding deep-learning as the foundation for equitable outcomes.

It describes the evolution of the district's work with the National Equity Project (NEP): from a small group who attended the Leading for Equity Institute to a district-wide, capacity-building approach through coaching, training, and deep instructional work. Troy School District is a member of the NEP Leading for Equity Redesign Network (LERN), which provides coaching, professional learning, and district partnerships. Learning Series 1, "Site Leadership for Equity and Belonging," is designed for principals and site-level administrators (assistant principals, deans) and may also benefit instructional coaches. The listed LERN Network districts are: Alameda Unified School District (CA), Burlington Area School District (WI), DeForest Area School District (WI), Dayton Public Schools (OH), LaGrange Elementary School District (IL), Michigan City Area Schools (IN), San Mateo Union High School District (CA), Troy School District (MI), Waukegan Community Unit School District (IL), and Waunakee Community School District (WI).

The District NEP LERN Team spans district leadership (Superintendent; Assistant Superintendents; Directors of Teaching and Learning, Special Education, ELD, and Early Childhood) and building leaders (elementary principal and teacher, K-5 literacy coordinator, middle school principal and teacher, high school principal, AP, and teacher, and the TCCHS principal).

The TSD Student Voice Project gathers reflections of student and alumni experiences to further the Equity and Inclusion work through short interviews used in staff professional learning; anonymous responses are read and used internally but cannot be included in the final project. The district currently has 60 responses reflecting a mix of positive and negative experiences, with next steps to read through them, reach out, capture students sharing experiences for professional learning, and resend the invitation to participate once school resumes.

Next steps requiring Board support include adopting updated language regarding acts of hate and bias in the student code of conduct, designing and implementing a reporting tool for TSD community members specific to acts of hate, bias, and discrimination, and communicating regular updates. Things to expect during the year include continued and expanded partnership with the National Equity Project; learning around implicit bias and anti-racist teaching; community conversations with students, staff, and families; the Student Voice Project; trauma-informed instruction; studying student data with teacher teams; reflecting on student discipline and behavior; partnership with outside experts; and sustaining deep-learning work through a guaranteed and viable curriculum.

The Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting review comments, dated August 2, 2020, prepared by the ASBO International Certificate of Excellence (COE) Review Team for Troy School District, Troy, Michigan, evaluating the district's Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2019. The document opens by stating it is the consensus of the Review Team to award the Certificate of Excellence, commending the district for its efforts and describing the CAFR as of high quality.

The comments are organized by section with page references. Under the introductory and financial sections, the numbered comments are: (Cover) a cover to the CAFR is not included though a title page is present, and both should be included in future submissions; (page i) in the second paragraph, third line, 'should' is stated twice and should be removed; (2) in the fourth paragraph the first sentence appears to be missing information and does not read correctly ('about the most District as a whole'); (3) a table shows a positive restricted net position but is labeled restricted (deficit) as a component of net position; (4) the last paragraph notes deferrals will be amortized through plan year 2019, which differs from the amortization table on page 3-27; (5) in the last paragraph the word 'between' is included twice; (6) the change in capital assets should be $27.2 million instead of $27.5 million; (7) in the first paragraph the debt limit does not agree with the table on page 6-14, noted as a repeat of the prior-year comment that the 2018 response said would be addressed in the 2020 audit report; (8) consider revising the reference to the accompanying notes at the bottom of each applicable page to 'basic financial statements' (2012 GAAFR, page 596); (9) it is difficult to determine how net investment in capital assets is calculated on the face of the statement of net position, so consider adding the calculation in the MD&A or footnotes (GASBS 34: 33; 2012 GAAFR, pages 300-303); and (10) it is unclear why the future amortization table would present amortization for 2019. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A slide-deck presentation, titled around "TSD Return to Learn," delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education at its special meeting on September 29, 2020, updating the District's pandemic reopening plan.

Goals: Three stated Return to Learn goals: (1) students return to face-to-face instruction as soon as possible; (2) safety and sustainability; and (3) consistent and flexible programming.

Process and framework: The Return to Learn process is grounded in the MI Return to School Roadmap, guidance from public health experts, and flexibility to changing conditions. Four key elements drive decisions: County Health Department Guidance, Safety Protocols, Budget, and Health Data. The District reports continued monitoring of Oakland County data in collaboration with the Oakland County Health Department (OCHD) and a new partnership with the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services. Agreements were reached with the Troy Education Association (TEA) related to the Return to Learn Road Map, covering safety and security protocols, the instructional model, and continued strides to support the most vulnerable populations.

Attendance/engagement (first four weeks): Elementary weekly attendance was 99.81%, 99.73%, 99.77%, and 99.86%. Secondary weekly attendance was 99.83%, 99.84%, 99.86%, and 99.93%.

Five Key Elements of the TSD Plan: (1) OneTroy Community at the Center; (2) Troy School District Curriculum; (3) Live Daily Instruction; (4) Meaningful Interactions with Teachers and Classmates; and (5) Streamlined Technology and Support.

Elementary hybrid plan: Described as a multifaceted decision that began with a common schedule with secondary, then diverged after reviewing data points (high numbers of virtual learners, elementary ability to cohort, and logistical concerns), challenging the district to think differently to meet students' instructional needs.

Parent selection results (a 4-week commitment): Elementary - Virtual 47%, Hybrid 44%, class-size range 18 to 3, average class size 10. Secondary - Virtual 44%, Hybrid 43%.

Secondary hybrid plan (grades 6-12): A consistent schedule using an A/B rotating day, 90-minute classes, Cohort A-K attending Monday/Tuesday, Cohort L-Z attending Thursday/Friday, and all students virtual on Wednesday. The bell schedule is aligned with the bussing schedule. At Athens High School (AHS) and Troy High School (THS), students dismiss before lunch; middle school students have lunch in the building. At the Troy Community College High School (TCCHS), students return for face-to-face instruction October 19th, with student support time in the morning, first bell 9:00 and last bell 2:10, breakfast and lunch provided in the building, and the opportunity to attend in-seat instruction four days a week (Monday/Tuesday/Thursday/Friday).

Timeline for Return to Learn Plan: October 5 - Kindergarten and 1st grade in-seat students report. October 12 - 2nd-3rd grade and 6th grade in-seat students report. What it is
The Agreement for CARES Act Distribution between Oakland County and the Troy School District (Agenda Item 5.G), the interlocal contract enabling the District to receive a share of the County's federal CARES Act funds.

Parties

- Entered pursuant to the Urban Cooperation Act of 1967, 1967 Public Act 7, MCL 124.501 et seq.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This document is the Agreement for CARES Act Distribution between Oakland County and the Troy School District, filed under Agenda Item 5.G for the October 20, 2020 Regular Meeting. It is the interlocal governmental contract required before the District can receive a portion of the County's federal CARES Act funds. The named parties are Oakland County, a Municipal and Constitutional Corporation located at 1200 North Telegraph Road, Pontiac, Michigan 48341 (the "County"), and the Troy School District, located at 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098 (the "School District"); each may be referred to individually as a Party and jointly as the Parties.

Purpose: The Parties enter into the Agreement pursuant to the Urban Cooperation Act of 1967, 1967 Public Act 7, MCL 124.501 et seq., for the purpose of the County distributing a portion of its CARES Act funds to the School District. The County has allocated a portion of its CARES Act funds to be distributed to school districts within Oakland County to assist them in meeting certain areas of need caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The agreement is made in consideration of the mutual promises, obligations, representations, and assurances of the Parties.

Definitions: The Agreement defines numerous terms, including Agreement, Claims, County, Day, School District, and School District Employee. Claims is defined broadly to cover alleged losses, complaints, demands, lawsuits, judgments, liabilities, penalties, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorney fees, witness fees, court costs, and settlement amounts) whether based on constitutional, statutory, regulatory, or common-law violations, in law or equity, tort or contract. County means Oakland County including all departments, divisions, the County Board of Commissioners, and its officials, employees, agents, and volunteers. Day means any calendar day beginning at 12:00 a.m. and ending at 11:59 p.m. School District Employee is defined to include employees, officers, directors, managers, trustees, volunteers, attorneys, contractors, subcontractors, and agents who use or have access to the Oakland Together Schools COVID Support funds, but expressly excludes an individual resident of the School District who receives an authorized distribution of those funds.

CARES Act funds means the money distributed to the County by the United States Department of Treasury pursuant to section 601(a) of the Social Security Act, as added by section 5001 of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act. The Oakland Together Schools COVID Support Fund (or "Oakland Together Schools" funds) means the portion of the CARES Act funds the County has allocated to school districts within Oakland County. The Expenditure Submission Form is the form the School District must complete and submit to the OCE prior to any disbursement of Oakland Together Schools funds. OCE means the Office of the Oakland County Executive, which includes the Chief Deputy and other Deputy County Executives. The Oversight Committee is the committee established by the Oakland County Board of Commissioners in the resolution allocating the Oakland Together Schools funds.

County Responsibilities: The OCE will review the School District's Expenditure Submission Form to determine whether the District is eligible to receive a distribution of Oakland Together Schools funds, in the OCE's discretion pursuant to the Coronavirus Relief Fund Guidance for State, Territorial, Local and Tribal Governments or other federal guidance, and may request supporting documentation. The extracted text is truncated at this point and does not include the remaining terms of the agreement.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is the audit results presentation prepared by Plante Moran for the Troy School District Board of Education covering the fiscal year ended June 30, 2020.

Key audit highlights: the 2020 financial statement audit resulted in an unmodified (clean) opinion; the 2020 federal program (single) audit also returned an unmodified opinion with no findings or questioned costs. The presentation confirms Bond and Sinking Fund compliance and Uniform Budget Act compliance, the adoption of GASB Statement 84 ("Fiduciary Activities") effective July 1, 2019, and receipt of the ASBO Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for 2019.

Governmental funds results (year ended June 30, 2020): General Fund revenue was $157,221,916 and expenditures were $156,870,348, an excess of revenue over expenditures of $351,568. Net transfers in were $500,000 and transfers out $248,351, producing net other financing sources of $251,649 and a net change in fund balance of +$603,217. The General Fund balance rose from $25,406,493 at the beginning of the year to $26,009,710 at year end, equal to 16.58% of total expenditures and other uses, or roughly 8.6 weeks (61 days) of operations. The 2019 Capital Projects Fund ran a $244,176 deficit, ending at $26,695,847. Total Nonmajor Funds showed revenue of $32,807,333 and expenditures of $49,373,068; with $6,100,000 face value of debt issued, a $117,488 premium, and $3,229,580 in proceeds from the sale of capital assets, nonmajor fund balances ended at $11,356,218.

General Fund revenue composition: local revenue $40,879,946 (26%), state source revenue $104,219,339 (66%), federal revenue $3,636,911 (2%), and interdistrict source revenue $8,485,720 (6%). An alternate breakdown lists the state portion of the foundation allowance at $83,661,291 (53%), property taxes $38,375,047 (25%), other state and local $31,548,667 (20%), and federal $3,636,911 (2%).

General Fund expenditures by object: salaries and employee benefits $128,878,409 (82%), purchased services $19,299,246 (12%), supplies $6,606,938 (4%), and other expenses $2,085,755 (2%). By function, direct instruction was 68.47%, indirect instruction 12.33%, general administration and business services 1.77%, school administration 5.20%, operations and maintenance 6.82%, pupil transportation 2.28%, central services 1.80%, community services 0.08%, and athletics 1.25%. The presentation notes the Oakland County average for direct instruction in FY19 was 61.48%.

Enrollment and funding: the February 2020 student count was 13,073, and the 2019-2020 foundation allowance was $9,315 per pupil, yielding total state aid of $121,774,995. A comparison of foundation revenue per pupil across Oakland County districts ranks Troy at $9,315, below Bloomfield Hills ($12,364), Birmingham ($12,284), Southfield ($11,331), Lamphere ($10,789), and Farmington ($10,405), and above West Bloomfield, Royal Oak, Novi, Walled Lake, Rochester, Waterford, and Huron Valley ($8,111). The deck closes with notes on 2020-2021 public education funding uncertainty, including the August 2020 Revenue Estimating Conference, the economic impact of the pandemic, MPSERS challenges, and changes in federal funding such as the Coronavirus Relief Fund.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This presentation, titled 'What Is a Board Member?', was delivered at the Troy School District Board of Education's October 20, 2020 meeting. It combines an educational overview of school board governance and ethics with a specific case presentation supporting the potential censure and disclaiming of acts of Trustee Elizabeth Hammond.

The governance section states that school board members are elected officials who must uphold the Michigan Constitution's mandate to provide free public elementary and secondary education, and it enumerates general powers a Board of Education may execute under the School Code — including educating pupils (K-12, preschool, adult ed), providing for student safety and welfare, acquiring and disposing of school property, matters involving the receipt and expenditure of school funds, and joint/cooperative agreements — while noting that board actions cannot conflict with or circumvent state prohibitions. It quotes the National School Boards Association Code of Ethics ('I will take no private action that will compromise the board or administration') and the Michigan Association of School Boards Board of Education Governance Standards endorsed by the Michigan State Board of Education, citing standards 3.a (a board member has no independent legal authority under Michigan law), 3.c (follows established policies and procedures), 3.d (supports Board decisions after a vote regardless of individual position), and 3.g (respects district structure and protocols). It references the TSD Policy Manual Section 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board, quoting the signed Code of Ethics acknowledging that a board member has no legal authority as an individual, that decisions require a majority vote at a public meeting, and commitments to confidentiality and a positive working relationship with the Superintendent.

On violations, the presentation defines censure (per Oxford Languages, the expressing of 'formal disapproval') as available by majority vote for violating federal or Michigan law, the Bylaws, or Board policy, or otherwise acting inconsistently with the office. It explains 'disclaiming acts of individual board members,' citing Section 1201 of the Revised School Code that trustees may exercise power only collectively at a regular or properly called special meeting, and stating that a disclaiming motion passed by a board majority alerts the community that an individual trustee's actions do not represent the will of the board.

The section titled 'ETHICS VIOLATIONS – TRUSTEE ELIZABETH HAMMOND' states the decision to publicly discuss the case for disclaiming and censure did not come lightly, and asserts the violations reflect a repeated pattern of behavior rather than isolated instances. It notes Trustee Hammond had been informally advised on at least three occasions: a President's letter dated October 2, 2019; a Board self-evaluation in January 2020; and a Special board meeting on September 29, 2020. It states her response was to disregard this advice. The presentation quotes a Hammond Facebook post to a Troy Parent Group dated Wednesday, September 23, 2020, in which she wrote that she supports parents' right to choose for their families during the governor's Phase 4 but does not believe an in-person option should 'throw science out the window,' asserting that 'THE CURRENT PLAN DOES NOT DO THIS AND PUTS THE ENTIRE COMMUNITY AT RISK,' and that the current scenario disadvantages students who remain at home and makes highly effective teaching virtually impossible.

What it is
Consideration item 10.C. (11.17.20) under "Other" - an Open Meetings Act resolution responding to recent changes restricting remote participation by public-body members.

Background / Whereas clauses
- Michigan Senate Bill 1108 of 2020 amended the Open Meetings Act to restrict reasons a public-body member may attend remotely, beginning January 1, 2021.
- Technology enabled districts to meet remotely during COVID-19 and ensure safe public participation.
- SB 1108 would allow remote attendance after December 31, 2021 only for absence due to military duty.
- Cites ongoing risks (contagious disease, flooding, tornadoes, terrorism) and the ADA Reasonable Accommodation clause for immune-compromised members.
- Asserts remote-attendance decisions are best made locally, not by the State Legislature.

Resolved (the Board):
- Urges the Legislature to amend SB 1108, Sec. 3a(b) to let local bodies set their own remote-participation policies (local control).
- Urges, at minimum, amending Sec. 3a(b) to indefinitely extend remote attendance for medical conditions, statewide/local emergencies or disasters, plus family emergencies and work obligations, in addition to military service.
- Directs the Board Secretary to transmit the resolution within five business days to Senator Mallory McMorrow, Representative Padma Kuppa, Oakland Schools Intermediate School District, and the Michigan Association of School Boards.

Vote
Roll call vote: Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb (Yes/No).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A board consideration cover sheet and suggested resolution for agenda item 10.C. (dated 11.17.20), under the "Other" section of the Troy Board of Education's regular meeting on November 17, 2020, addressing recent changes to Michigan's Open Meetings Act (OMA) concerning electronic meetings and remote participation.

The recommended action is to accept the resolution as presented. The whereas clauses recite that: Michigan Senate Bill 1108 of 2020 amended the State's Open Meetings Act to restrict the reasons a member of a public body may attend a public meeting remotely beginning January 1, 2021; advancing technology enabled school districts across the State to meet remotely during the COVID-19 pandemic, to develop and implement plans to educate students safely and effectively, and to ensure safe and effective public participation; the restrictions in SB 1108 allow remote attendance after December 31, 2021 only for absence due to military duty; threats to public health and other disasters (contagious diseases, flooding, tornadoes, acts of terrorism, or other causes) will not vanish on December 31, 2020 and could make it unsafe or impossible for public bodies to meet in person; not allowing an immune-compromised member to participate remotely would be a clear violation of the Reasonable Accommodation clause of the federal Americans with Disabilities Act; and decisions about when remote attendance is merited are best determined by the local body and community rather than the State Legislature.

The operative resolutions provide that the Troy School District Board of Education: (1) Urges the Legislature to ideally amend Senate Bill 1108, Sec. 3a(b) to include a provision requiring local public bodies to set their own policies regarding remote meeting participation based on the needs and priorities of their own local communities rather than dictating universal policy statewide without regard to local control; (2) Urges the Legislature to, at a minimum, amend Senate Bill 1108, Sec. 3a(b) to extend indefinitely its provisions allowing remote attendance to accommodate absence due to a medical condition or a statewide or local state of emergency or state of disaster, in addition to military service, and add accommodations for family emergencies and work obligations; and (3) Directs the Board Secretary to transmit copies of this resolution within five business days of adoption to Senator Mallory McMorrow, Representative Padma Kuppa, Oakland Schools Intermediate School District, and the Michigan Association of School Boards.

The resolution includes blank lines for the moving and supporting members and specifies a roll-call vote listing board members Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, and Gottlieb, with tally lines for Yes and No. The completed vote result is not recorded on this cover sheet.

Addendum 1 to the Troy School District's Bid No. 9909, Exterior Signage at Athens High School, Learning Center, and Early Childcare Center, is a procurement clarification document issued as part of the district's competitive bidding process. It states that it is issued as modifications to the previously issued RFP to provide clarifications to the scope of work, that it supersedes the original RFP, and that together with the RFP it becomes the bid documents. The bid due date is expressly restated as 11:00 AM Wednesday, November 4, 2020, and marked unchanged.

Under General Information, the addendum directs bidders to email purchasingoffice@troy.k12.mi.us or use Buildingconnected.com for questions. Bidders wishing to schedule a job-site visit are told to contact Mark Paulus at (248) 880-6791 and are instructed not to visit the building without a scheduled visit. It emphasizes that Athens High School, the Learning Center, and the Early Childcare Center are school buildings and that all rules and laws for a school building must be followed.

The Questions and Answers section contains four items. First, the overall height of the signs at the Learning Center and Early Childcare Center shall be 6 feet 0 inches. Second, power will be brought to the new signs by another contractor and is not included in this bid package; the bidder on this package is responsible for making the final connection from the electrical to the sign. Third, in response to a question about specification article 2.3.B, which describes new display housing dimensions of approximately 3 feet 8 inches tall by 7 feet 4 inches wide, retrofit display housing dimensions of approximately 4 feet 2 inches tall by 7 feet 4 inches wide, and (article 2.3.B.9) a full LED matrix measuring a minimum of 60 pixel rows high by 150 pixel columns wide, the district answers that the LED matrix should be the same for all three signs even though the housing dimensions are different. Fourth, regarding the upper illuminated cabinets, the district answers that the size of all of the upper illuminated cabinets is 18 inches tall by 7 feet 4 inches wide and should match the depth of the LED message center, which shall not exceed 7 inches. What it is
A Business Office memorandum (4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098) dated Friday, October 30, 2020, from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, to Superintendent Rich Machesky, providing a three-tier transportation financial analysis to support decision-making.

Route impact
- A three-tier system would allow moving school bell times.
- General education routes: from 32 (2020-21) to 46; special education: from 23 to 26.
- Total routes rise from 55 to 72.

Bus fleet impact
- Current fleet: 71 buses - 32 general education, 23 special education, 16 spares.

Financial impact
- General education routes: 14 additional x 180 days x $244.42 = $615,938.
- Special education routes: 3 additional x 180 days x $292.28 = $157,831.
- General education fuel: 10,000 miles/year x 14 runs x $1.30/gallon at 6 mpg = $30,333.
- Special education fuel: 15,000 miles/year x 3 runs x $1.30/gallon at 6 mpg = $9,750.
- Annual transportation operational cost increase: $813,852.

Additional considerations
Figures are based on 2019-20 data; 2021-22 changes, bell times, and a nationwide bus-driver shortage could affect efficiency and staffing.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This document is a memorandum on Business Office letterhead (4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098; Phone 248.823.4022, Fax 248.823.4013), dated Friday, October 30, 2020, from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, to Rich Machesky, Superintendent, regarding a 3-tier Transportation Financial Analysis. West presents the operational and financial impact of implementing a three-tier bus system to assist in the decision-making process.

On route impact, the memo explains that moving to a three-tier system would allow the district to move school bell times and would require 46 general education buses and 26 special education buses to cover current routes. A comparison table shows general education routes increasing from 32 in 2020-21 to 46 under three-tier requirements, special education routes increasing from 23 to 26, and total routes increasing from 55 to 72.

On bus fleet impact, the district currently has a fleet of 71 buses, of which 32 are designated for general education routes and 23 for special education routes, leaving 16 spares. On an average day, 6 buses are being worked on in some manner, so 10 are available for athletics, field trips, and extracurricular needs.

On financial impact, the memo itemizes the incremental costs. General Education Routes: 14 additional routes multiplied by 180 days multiplied by $244.42 per route equals $615,938. Special Education Routes: 3 additional routes multiplied by 180 days multiplied by $292.28 per route equals $157,831. General Education Fuel: 10,000 miles per year multiplied by 14 additional runs multiplied by $1.30 per gallon at 6 miles per gallon equals $30,333. Special Education Fuel: 15,000 miles per year multiplied by 3 additional runs multiplied by $1.30 per gallon at 6 miles per gallon equals $9,750. The stated Annual Transportation Operational Cost Increase totals $813,852.

Under Additional Considerations, West notes that the analysis is based on data from the 2019-20 school year, including student enrollment, riders, special education needs, and school building boundaries, and that changes are expected for the 2021-22 school year which may result in greater efficiencies or require additional resources. He observes that school bell times will also be a factor in determining the number of routes needed, and cautions about the challenges of recruiting and retaining the appropriate level of workforce given a nationwide shortage of bus drivers. The memorandum is an internal financial planning document rather than an action item with a vote.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This bid tabulation covers the Troy School District's School Bus Acquisition for the 2020-21 School Year and compares proposals from three vendors: Hoekstra Transportation, Holland, and Midwest-Transit. The bus specifications and requirements span five categories: 77 Passenger Conventional (quantity of 4), 77 Passenger Conventional with luggage (quantity of 4), 84 Passenger Rear Engine (quantity of 4), 53 Passenger Special Needs with Integrated Child Seating in 8 rows (quantity of 2), and 53 Passenger Special Needs with Integrated Child Seating in 3 rows (quantity of 2).

For each vendor the tabulation lists the extended price per category and a grand total. Hoekstra Transportation bid $377,272.00 for the 77 Passenger Conventional, $383,496.00 for the 77 Passenger Conventional with luggage, $512,980.00 for the 84 Passenger Rear Engine, $200,868.00 for the 8-row 53 Passenger Special Needs, and $212,660.00 for the 3-row 53 Passenger Special Needs, for a total of $1,687,276.00. Holland bid $376,144.00, $384,128.00, $519,204.00, $210,234.00, and $221,636.00, respectively, for a total of $1,711,346.00. Midwest-Transit bid $391,096.00, $400,064.00, $504,860.00, $210,564.00, and $215,662.00, respectively, for a total of $1,722,246.00.

Hoekstra Transportation has the lowest overall total at $1,687,276.00, roughly $24,000 below Holland and about $35,000 below Midwest-Transit, even though it is not the lowest on every individual line (for example, Holland is lower on the 77 Passenger Conventional at $376,144.00, and Midwest-Transit is lower on the 84 Passenger Rear Engine at $504,860.00). This tabulation is the supporting document for the district's recommendation, detailed in the accompanying Purchasing Department memo and board resolution, to award the 2020-21 school bus purchase to Hoekstra Transportation for $1,687,276.00 under the 2014 Bond Series 3 school bus replacement program.
